AGA-ATROPHIC.title: Diagnosis and management of atrophic gastritis

claims.text: Many patients have no symptoms
Upper abdominal pain or discomfort
Nausea or vomiting
Early satiety or excessive fullness after eating
Loss of appetite or weight loss
Black or tarry stool, blood or coffee-ground material in vomit, fatigue, dyspnea, or light-headedness may indicate gastric bleeding
Helicobacter pylori infection
Long-term exposure to NSAIDs, alcohol, or bile reflux
Autoimmune disease
Critical illness, sepsis, severe injury, or burns
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with gastric biopsies can diagnose gastritis, determine its cause, and assess complications
Stool antigen or urea breath testing can identify Helicobacter pylori infection
Acute gastritis develops suddenly and lasts a short time
Gastric biopsy must show inflammation rather than mucosal injury with little or no inflammation
Chronic gastritis develops slowly and lasts a long time
Helicobacter pylori and autoimmune gastritis are common chronic forms
Gastric histology shows chronic inflammation without the gland loss or intestinal metaplasia that defines atrophic gastritis
claims.derivation: Non-atrophic branch is the explicit complement of the AGA histopathologic definition of atrophic gastritis.

claims.text: Evidence of Helicobacter pylori supports a common cause of chronic non-atrophic gastritis
Histopathology confirms loss of gastric glands, with or without intestinal metaplasia, in chronic inflammation
Intestinal metaplasia on gastric histology almost always implies atrophic gastritis
Endoscopic features may include pale thinned mucosa, increased vascular visibility, and loss of gastric folds
Iron deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, or pernicious anemia may accompany corpus-predominant or autoimmune atrophic gastritis
Autoimmune gastritis and associated autoimmune thyroid disease
